q.s: Which glial-mediated process during sleep is thought to clear metabolic waste products from the brain?
q.e: Glial cells drive glymphatic clearance of metabolites during sleep — part of the “biochemical refreshment” function of sleep.

q.s: Declarative memory consolidation is most closely associated with which sleep feature?
q.e: Declarative memory consolidation is linked to NREM (spindles); procedural and emotional memory processing is linked to REM.

q.s: Procedural and emotional memory processing is predominantly associated with which sleep stage?
q.e: REM sleep supports procedural and emotional memory processing and affect regulation.

q.s: Growth hormone is secreted predominantly during:
o: N1 sleep at each cycle transition
REM sleep in the final third of the night
Early slow-wave sleep, in the first hours after sleep onset
q.e: The main GH pulse occurs in early slow-wave (N3) sleep, concentrated in the first third of the night.

q.s: Which hormone is described as being released in the late evening rather than during slow-wave sleep?
q.e: Thyroid hormone release is described as a late-evening event; GH is linked to early SWS.

q.s: Sleep-related regulation of appetite involves which hormone pair?
q.e: Sleep helps maintain leptin/ghrelin balance; fragmentation lowers leptin and raises ghrelin, increasing hunger.

q.s: Which statement about the relationship between sleep and rest is correct?
o: Sleep differs from rest only by the presence of eye closure
Sleep is qualitatively distinct from rest and is orchestrated by distinct neuronal networks
Sleep and quiet rest are physiologically equivalent states
Rest provides the same memory consolidation as sleep
q.e: The textbook definition emphasises that sleep is a complex physiological state qualitatively distinct from rest.

q.s: Which of the following is NOT generally listed as a health function of normal sleep?
o: Permanent elimination of the homeostatic sleep drive
q.e: Sleep dissipates sleep pressure each night, but the homeostatic drive rebuilds with time awake; it is not eliminated.

q.s: Anabolic dominance, protein synthesis and tissue repair during sleep describe which function?
q.e: Restoration and repair are core functions, with protein synthesis and cell/tissue repair favoured during sleep.

q.s: Which emotional function is most specifically attributed to REM sleep?
o: Processing of affect and emotional regulation
q.e: REM-dependent processing of affect underpins sleep’s role in emotional regulation.

q.s: Spindle density in N2 has been observed to increase after:
q.e: Spindle density rises after learning a new task, linking N2 spindles to memory consolidation.

q.s: Melatonin secretion is principally controlled by:
o: The light–dark cycle acting via the suprachiasmatic nucleus
q.e: Pineal melatonin is under light–dark control via the SCN and is suppressed by light.

q.s: Which metabolic benefit is attributed to adequate sleep?
q.e: Sleep supports metabolic regulation, including insulin sensitivity; sleep loss promotes insulin resistance.

q.s: The “biochemical refreshment” function of sleep refers chiefly to:
o: Increased skeletal muscle tone during REM
Restoration of synaptic and neuronal function, glycogen restoration and metabolite clearance
Elevation of core temperature set point
q.e: Biochemical refreshment covers synaptic/neuronal function, glymphatic clearance, glycogen restoration and neurogenesis.

q.s: Which immune-related statement about sleep is most accurate?
o: Sleep contributes to immune function and its disruption may impair it
Immune function is enhanced by chronic sleep restriction
Immune effects occur only during REM sleep
Sleep has no measurable effect on immune function
q.e: Immune function and metabolic regulation are among the recognised health benefits of normal sleep.

q.s: A patient asks why sleep is needed for children’s growth. The best explanation is that sleep:
o: Suppresses growth hormone to conserve energy
Facilitates growth via hormone release and protein synthesis, especially in slow-wave sleep
Increases thyroid hormone only during REM
q.e: Growth is facilitated through GH release in SWS and protein synthesis.

q.s: Possible learning of simple tasks or behaviours during sleep is listed among sleep’s benefits. Which stage feature is most associated with motor/procedural learning?
q.e: Procedural (motor) learning is associated with REM sleep.

q.s: Which hormones are listed as being released during sleep in addition to growth hormone?
q.e: Hormone regulation in sleep includes GH, prolactin, testosterone and PTH.

q.s: In the two-process model of sleep regulation, Process S refers to:
o: The circadian oscillator in the suprachiasmatic nucleus
The homeostatic sleep drive that accumulates with time awake
q.e: Process S is homeostatic sleep pressure; Process C is the circadian rhythm.

q.s: The principal candidate mediator of homeostatic sleep pressure is:
q.e: Adenosine accumulates with wakefulness and is the leading candidate mediator of Process S; caffeine antagonises it.

q.s: The master circadian clock is located in the:
q.e: The SCN is the endogenous ~24 h oscillator; the pineal gland produces melatonin under its control.

q.s: Light entrains the circadian clock via the:
q.e: Light information reaches the SCN through the retinohypothalamic tract.

q.s: Orexin (hypocretin)-producing neurons are located in the:
q.e: Orexin/hypocretin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus promote wakefulness; their loss causes narcolepsy type 1.

q.s: Which pairing of wake-promoting neurotransmitter and source nucleus is correct?
q.e: Noradrenaline arises from the locus coeruleus; serotonin from raphe; histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus.

q.s: NREM sleep is promoted by GABA and galanin released from the:
q.e: VLPO neurons release GABA and galanin to inhibit arousal systems and promote NREM sleep.

q.s: During REM sleep, which neuronal activity is maximal?
o: Orexinergic neurons of the lateral hypothalamus
Cholinergic “REM-on” neurons of the pedunculopontine/laterodorsal tegmentum
q.e: REM is driven by cholinergic REM-on neurons while monoaminergic and orexinergic activity reaches its nadir.

q.s: Why do serotonergic and noradrenergic antidepressants tend to suppress REM sleep?
q.e: REM requires monoaminergic activity to fall; drugs boosting serotonin/noradrenaline therefore suppress REM.

q.s: The approximate proportion of adult sleep spent in REM is:
q.e: Adults spend roughly 20–25% of sleep in REM and 75–80% in NREM.

q.s: The approximate proportion of adult sleep spent in stage N2 is:
q.e: N2 is the largest single stage at about 45–55% of total sleep.

q.s: Sleep spindles (11–16 Hz) and K-complexes are characteristic of:
q.e: Spindles and K-complexes define stage N2.

q.s: Stage N1 is characterised by:
o: Replacement of alpha rhythm by low-voltage mixed-frequency activity, with vertex sharp waves
q.e: N1 (2–5% of sleep) is transitional: alpha is replaced by low-voltage mixed frequency activity, with vertex sharp waves.

q.s: Which EEG feature is characteristic of REM sleep?
q.e: REM shows desynchronised EEG, sawtooth waves, theta activity and rapid eye movements.

q.s: The alpha rhythm of relaxed wakefulness has a frequency of:
q.e: Alpha is 8–13 Hz; spindles 11–16 Hz; theta 3–7 Hz; delta is slow (<2 Hz).

q.s: Since the AASM 2007 scoring rules, the former Rechtschaffen & Kales stages 3 and 4 are combined as:
q.e: Stages 3 and 4 merged into N3 (slow-wave sleep); the scheme is now N1/N2/N3/R.

q.s: Slow-wave sleep (N3) is concentrated in:
o: The first third of the night
The middle of the night only
The final third of the night
q.e: N3 dominates early cycles; REM periods lengthen and dominate the last third of the night.

q.s: The first sleep cycle typically lasts about 70–100 minutes; subsequent cycles last:
q.e: Later cycles last ~90–120 min, giving 4–6 cycles per night.

q.s: Normal REM latency from sleep onset is approximately:
q.e: REM latency is about 90 minutes; very short latencies (SOREMPs) suggest narcolepsy or sleep deprivation.

q.s: Which physiological change is characteristic of REM rather than NREM sleep?
o: Reduced sympathetic activity below waking levels
Blood pressure rises up to 30% and fluctuates
q.e: In REM, BP rises (up to 30%) and fluctuates, sympathetic activity is high, breathing is irregular and muscle tone is absent.

q.s: Which function is effectively absent during REM sleep?
q.e: Thermoregulation is suspended in REM (no shivering or sweating).

q.s: In NREM sleep compared with wakefulness:
o: Heart rate, blood pressure and sympathetic activity fall
Sympathetic activity rises markedly above waking
Respiration becomes irregular with central pauses
q.e: NREM is a state of autonomic quiescence: HR, BP and sympathetic activity fall and breathing is regular.

q.s: Upper airway resistance during sleep compared with wakefulness:
o: Increases in both NREM and REM sleep
q.e: Upper airway resistance increases from wake in both NREM and REM sleep.

q.s: During sleep, renal function normally shows:
o: Reduced sodium, potassium, chloride and calcium excretion with concentrated urine
Increased urine flow, making nocturia normal
q.e: Urine output falls and becomes concentrated during sleep, so nocturia is abnormal and a recognised OSA symptom.

q.s: Approximately what percentage of vivid dream recall comes from awakenings in REM sleep?
q.e: About 80% of vivid dream recall follows REM awakenings.

q.s: The morning peak in myocardial infarction is linked to:
o: The heart rate and blood pressure surge on awakening
Reduced cerebral blood flow in NREM
q.e: The awakening HR/BP surge is thought to underlie the morning MI peak — a surge repeated many times a night in OSA.

q.s: Which stage has the highest arousal threshold of all NREM stages?
q.e: N3 is the deepest NREM stage, with the highest arousal threshold; disorders of arousal arise from it.

q.s: Adult respiratory rate during sleep is typically:
q.e: Adults breathe 12–20/min asleep; infants and young children up to 30–60/min.

q.s: Upper airway narrowing at sleep onset in a healthy person is best described as:
o: A pathological event that always indicates OSA
A normal physiological event caused by withdrawal of tonic drive to the dilator muscles
q.e: Narrowing is normal; in OSA it is exaggerated by combined abnormal anatomy and physiology into repetitive collapse.

q.s: The principal upper airway dilator muscle responsible for resisting inspiratory collapse is the:
q.e: Tonic and phasic genioglossus activity holds the airway open in wakefulness; this compensation is withdrawn at sleep onset.

q.s: The pharynx behaves mechanically as a:
q.e: The collapsible pharyngeal segment is modelled as a Starling resistor; collapsibility is quantified by Pcrit.

q.s: Pcrit (critical closing pressure) in a healthy individual is typically:
q.e: Healthy airways have negative Pcrit; in OSA it shifts toward positive values — more positive means more collapsible.

q.s: Using Pcrit, moderate anatomical impairment is defined as:
The most common sites of upper airway obstruction in adult OSA are:
q.e: Obstruction can occur from nasopharynx to larynx, but retropalatal and retroglossal sites are commonest.

q.s: In the PALM phenotyping framework, “A” stands for:
q.e: PALM: Pcrit (passive anatomy), Arousal threshold, Loop gain, Muscle responsiveness.

q.s: Approximately what proportion of OSA patients have at least one non-anatomical trait impairment?
q.e: About 70% have ≥1 non-anatomical impairment, supporting phenotype-directed therapy.

q.s: High loop gain in OSA describes:
o: A high threshold for arousal from sleep
Oversensitive ventilatory control causing overshoot and undershoot of ventilation
q.e: High loop gain (~36%) produces unstable periodic breathing that promotes both central and obstructive events.

q.s: A low respiratory arousal threshold (present in ~37%) would theoretically be targeted with:
q.e: Raising the arousal threshold with eszopiclone is the targeted approach; acetazolamide targets loop gain.

q.s: Which therapy targets high loop gain?
q.e: Acetazolamide and oxygen stabilise ventilatory control in the high loop gain endotype.

q.s: Poor upper airway muscle responsiveness (~36% of patients) might be targeted with:
o: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation, myofunctional therapy or atomoxetine + oxybutynin
q.e: Muscle-responsiveness therapies aim to recruit dilators: HNS, myofunctional therapy and noradrenergic–antimuscarinic drugs.

q.s: Why might a correctly fitted and fully titrated mandibular advancement device fail in a patient?
o: It is an anatomical intervention that does not systematically change loop gain or arousal threshold
It increases loop gain in all patients
q.e: MADs improve passive anatomy only; patients driven by non-anatomical traits or very positive Pcrit may not respond.

q.s: Which obesity-related mechanism contributes to airway collapsibility?
o: Increased lung volume stiffening the pharynx
Reduced functional residual capacity lessening caudal tracheal traction on the pharynx
q.e: Obesity reduces FRC and chest wall compliance, decreasing caudal traction, and loads the airway with parapharyngeal fat.

q.s: Rostral fluid shift contributes to OSA by:
o: Displacing fluid from the legs to the neck on lying down, narrowing the pharynx
q.e: Recumbency shifts fluid rostrally into neck tissues, an important mechanism in heart failure and oedematous states.

q.s: Which craniofacial feature is a recognised anatomical risk factor for OSA?
o: Retrognathia with an inferiorly positioned hyoid
Prognathic mandible with a high hyoid
q.e: Retrognathia, micrognathia, maxillary constriction, steep mandibular plane and a low hyoid are recognised risks.

q.s: In adults with moderate anatomical impairment (the largest group), approximately what proportion also have ≥1 non-anatomical impairment?
q.e: ~64% have ≥1 non-anatomical trait (favouring combination therapy); ~36% do not (anatomical intervention alone may suffice).

q.s: In the CPAP “dial-down” technique, a peak inspiratory flow of at least 30% of baseline indicates:
q.e: Higher PIF on dial-down corresponds to a more negative Pcrit, i.e. a less collapsible airway.

q.s: The awake upper airway collapsibility index is calculated as:
q.e: Higher % collapsibility correlates with higher sleeping Pcrit; it takes ~10 minutes and is easier than formal Pcrit measurement.

q.s: Objective PSG evidence of OSA without symptoms is termed:
o: OSA (alone), whereas with symptoms it is OSA syndrome
q.e: OSA refers to PSG evidence; OSA syndrome denotes PSG evidence plus symptoms.

q.s: Chronic snoring vibration may contribute to OSA progression through:
o: Pharyngeal sensory neuropathy impairing reflex dilator responses
q.e: Pharyngeal sensory neuropathy from chronic vibration is a recognised “other” pathophysiological factor.

q.s: Which statement about mandibular advancement and the PALM traits is correct?
o: It works mainly by increasing genioglossus EMG
It reduces collapsibility dose-dependently without systematically changing genioglossus function
q.e: The primary mode of action is improved passive pharyngeal anatomy.

q.s: The term sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) encompasses:
o: A spectrum from increased airflow resistance and snoring through hypopnoea to apnoea
q.e: SDB is a group of disorders of breathing during sleep spanning increased resistance, heavy snoring, hypopnoea and apnoea.

q.s: Nasal obstruction (e.g. septal deviation, turbinate hypertrophy) contributes to SDB by:
o: Increasing resistance, promoting mouth breathing and reducing PAP tolerance
q.e: Nasal pathology raises upstream resistance, promotes mouth breathing and impairs PAP tolerance.

q.s: In the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort (1993), the prevalence of AHI >5 in middle-aged men was approximately:
q.e: Young et al. (1993): AHI >5 in 24% of men and 9% of women.

q.s: In the Wisconsin cohort, the prevalence of AHI >5 with daytime sleepiness (OSA syndrome) was approximately:
More recent US estimates (2007–2010) of moderate–severe OSA prevalence are approximately:
q.e: Peppard et al. reported moderate–severe OSA in ~13% of men and ~6% of women.

q.s: Global estimates suggest how many adults aged 30–69 have moderate–severe OSA?
q.e: Benjafield et al. (2019): ~936 million with any OSA and ~425 million with moderate–severe disease.

q.s: The main reason published OSA prevalence figures differ between studies is:
o: Different hypopnoea definitions, AHI thresholds, symptom requirements and population characteristics
q.e: Always quote a prevalence with its definition (3% vs 4% hypopnoea rule, AHI cut-off, symptom requirement).

q.s: Which comorbidity is listed as most predictive of OSA?
o: Obesity, hypertension, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes
q.e: Obesity, hypertension, CVD (especially ischaemic heart disease) and T2DM are the key predictive comorbidities.

q.s: The relationship between obesity and OSA is best described as:
o: Bidirectional, with sleep fragmentation promoting weight gain via appetite hormones
q.e: Fragmentation lowers leptin and raises ghrelin, increasing appetite for calorie-dense food and reducing activity.

q.s: Which long-term consequence is associated with untreated OSA?
q.e: Long-term consequences include neurocognitive impairment, metabolic syndrome, hypertension and CVD.

q.s: Approximately what proportion of US adults has been estimated to have OSA in broader estimates?
q.e: Estimates of ~17% are commonly cited, rising to ~38% depending on definitions.

q.s: The prevalence of paediatric OSA is approximately:
In children with Down syndrome, moderate–severe OSA (AHI >5) is found in approximately:
q.e: Prevalence is ~50% at AHI >5 and 69% at AHI >1, far above the general paediatric population.

q.s: An AHI of ≥15 is significant because it is the level at which:
o: Insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, vascular disease and mortality risks rise materially
q.e: AHI ≥15 marks a material rise in metabolic and vascular risk, which is why it qualifies as OSA without symptoms.

q.s: In the Wisconsin cohort, prevalence of AHI >15 was approximately:
Which statement best explains why OSA is under-recognised in women?
o: OSA does not occur before menopause
Women more often present atypically with insomnia, fatigue and mood symptoms
q.e: Atypical presentation (insomnia, fatigue, mood) leads to under-diagnosis in women.

q.s: Severe sleep-disordered breathing is associated with increased risk of which renal condition?
q.e: SDB is highly prevalent in CKD and severe SDB increases CKD risk.

q.s: Which oral condition has an emerging bidirectional relationship with OSA via inflammatory markers?
q.e: Periodontitis and OSA share inflammatory markers in an emerging bidirectional relationship.

q.s: The global burden figure of ~936 million refers to:
o: Adults aged 30–69 with OSA of any severity (AHI ≥5)
q.e: Benjafield 2019: 936 million any OSA; 425 million moderate–severe.

q.s: A 10% increase in body weight is associated with an approximate AHI increase of:
q.e: Peppard 2000: 10% weight gain → ~32% AHI rise; 10% loss → ~26% fall.

q.s: A 10% reduction in body weight is associated with an approximate AHI reduction of:
q.e: Weight loss of 10% lowers AHI by about 26%.

q.s: The most important and only readily reversible major risk factor for OSA is:
q.e: Obesity is the key modifiable risk factor; sex, age and craniofacial structure are not readily modifiable.

q.s: The male-to-female ratio for OSA in adults is approximately:
q.e: Male predominance is ~2–3:1, narrowing with age and after menopause.

q.s: Why does the gender gap in OSA narrow after the menopause?
o: Loss of oestrogen’s protective effect plus weight gain and central fat redistribution
q.e: Post-menopausal loss of hormonal protection and central adiposity increase OSA risk in women.

q.s: OSA prevalence with ageing typically:
o: Rises, peaking around 60 years, possibly plateauing in very advanced age
q.e: Prevalence rises with age to about 60, then may plateau or decline in the very old.

q.s: In children, the dominant OSA risk factor shifts from adenotonsillar hypertrophy (peak 2–8 years) to which factor in adolescence?
q.e: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy dominates early childhood; obesity becomes more important in adolescence.

q.s: Which endocrine condition is a recognised risk factor for OSA?
q.e: Acromegaly (macroglossia, soft tissue growth), hypothyroidism and PCOS are recognised endocrine risks.

q.s: Neck circumference associated with higher OSA risk in men is greater than:
q.e: >43 cm (17 in) in men and >40 cm (16 in) in women indicates increased risk.

q.s: Neck circumference associated with higher OSA risk in women is greater than:
q.e: The female threshold is >40 cm (16 in).

q.s: Alcohol increases OSA severity mainly by:
o: Reducing pharyngeal dilator tone and blunting arousal responses
Increasing REM in the first half of the night
q.e: Alcohol reduces dilator tone and blunts arousal, lengthening and worsening events.

q.s: Smoking contributes to SDB principally through:
o: Upper airway inflammation, with nocturnal nicotine withdrawal causing arousals
q.e: Smoking causes upper airway inflammation, and nicotine withdrawal through the night fragments sleep.

q.s: Which sleeping position typically increases AHI in adults?
q.e: Gravity-dependent posterior displacement of the tongue and soft palate makes supine sleep the worst position.

q.s: Which of the following is NOT a recognised risk factor for OSA?
q.e: Retrognathia, not prognathism, is the recognised craniofacial risk factor.

q.s: Which cardiovascular condition is also listed as a risk factor that can predispose to OSA (via fluid shift and ventilatory instability)?
q.e: Heart failure predisposes to OSA and CSA through rostral fluid shift and high loop gain.

q.s: A 48-year-old man reports gaining 15 kg over 3 years, with worsening snoring. The most accurate counselling statement is:
o: Weight loss will certainly cure his OSA
Only surgery can help weight-related OSA
Weight gain is likely to have worsened his SDB, and weight loss could reduce AHI but rarely cures it alone
q.e: Weight change has a strong dose–response effect on AHI, but weight loss is hard to sustain and often not curative.

q.s: Which nasal condition is a recognised OSA risk factor?
q.e: Nasal congestion, rhinitis and sinusitis increase resistance and are listed risk factors.

q.s: Which statement about genetics and OSA is correct?
o: Family history of OSA is a recognised risk factor
Family history only matters in children
q.e: Familial clustering reflects inherited craniofacial structure, obesity and ventilatory control.

q.s: Which nocturnal symptom is characteristic of OSA?
o: An urge to move the legs relieved by movement
q.e: Choking/gasping awakenings, witnessed apnoeas and loud snoring are classic nocturnal features.

q.s: Why is nocturia considered a symptom of OSA?
o: Nocturia is normal in all adults
Urine production normally falls in sleep, so nocturia is abnormal; OSA increases nocturnal natriuresis
Nocturia is caused by mandibular advancement
q.e: Normal sleep concentrates urine; OSA-related pressure swings and atrial stretch increase nocturnal urine output.

q.s: Which daytime symptom is typical of adult OSA?
o: Morning headache and dry mouth on waking
q.e: Morning headache, dry mouth, sleepiness, fatigue and poor concentration are typical daytime features.

q.s: Which statement about asymptomatic OSA is correct?
o: Symptoms are required for an OSA diagnosis at any AHI
Sympathetic activity and arterial pressure may be elevated even without symptoms
Asymptomatic patients always have mild disease
q.e: Severe disease may be asymptomatic yet still carry cardiovascular risk — the basis for treating AHI ≥15 regardless of symptoms.

q.s: Which presentation is more typical of OSA in children than adults?
o: Morning headache as the main complaint
Inattention, hyperactivity, irritability and learning problems
q.e: Children present behaviourally rather than sleepily — features that can mimic ADHD.

q.s: The most common reason for an adult to attend a sleep clinic because of someone else is:
o: Socially disruptive snoring ± witnessed apnoeas affecting the bed partner
q.e: The effect on the bed partner is one of three main reasons adults attend.

q.s: Which of the following is NOT a typical symptom of OSA?
q.e: Cataplexy is pathognomonic of narcolepsy type 1, not OSA.

q.s: Reduced libido and impotence in OSA are best described as:
o: Side effects of oral appliance therapy
q.e: Reduced libido and impotence are listed daytime symptoms of OSA.

q.s: Which statement about snoring as a symptom is correct?
o: Snoring neither rules OSA in nor out
q.e: About one third of OSA patients do not snore and one third of snorers have no OSA.

q.s: A 52-year-old woman reports insomnia, fatigue and low mood but no witnessed apnoeas. The most appropriate statement is:
o: OSA is excluded because she has no witnessed apnoeas
OSA should still be considered, as women often present atypically
q.e: Women frequently present with insomnia, fatigue and mood complaints, leading to under-diagnosis.

q.s: Which group requires urgent assessment and explicit driving advice when OSA is suspected?
o: Commercial drivers or those reporting sleepiness while driving
Retired patients who do not drive
q.e: Suspected OSA with driving sleepiness or in safety-critical work requires urgent assessment.

q.s: Restless sleep and night sweats in an adult snorer are best interpreted as:
q.e: Restless unrefreshing sleep and night sweats are listed nocturnal OSA symptoms.

q.s: Which of the following is a recognised oral sign associated with SDB?
o: Dry mouth on waking due to mouth breathing
q.e: Mouth breathing from nasal obstruction or jaw opening produces morning dry mouth.

q.s: Which statement about the Epworth score in OSA is correct?
o: Many OSA patients are not detectably sleepy, so a normal ESS does not exclude OSA
q.e: The ESS correlates poorly with AHI and must never be used alone.

q.s: Which group of symptoms most suggests concern about the long-term consequences of OSA?
o: Partner-witnessed apnoeas prompting concern about cardiovascular disease, stroke and driving safety
q.e: Suspicion of OSA, often after witnessed apnoeas, with concern about consequences is one of the three attendance triggers.

q.s: Tooth grinding and excessive salivation at night in a snorer may be:
o: Nocturnal features reported in OSA patients
q.e: Salivation and tooth grinding are listed among nocturnal OSA features; bruxism commonly co-occurs.

q.s: Which cardiovascular condition is particularly associated with OSA and often difficult to control until OSA is treated?
q.e: OSA is a recognised cause of resistant hypertension; CPAP may improve BP control.

q.s: Which arrhythmia is notably linked with untreated OSA and may be harder to control?
q.e: OSA is associated with atrial fibrillation (and ventricular tachycardia) that may be difficult to control.

q.s: Experimental sleep restriction and disruption of slow-wave and REM sleep has been shown to:
o: Have no effect on pain perception
Lower pain thresholds and reduce the analgesic potency of morphine
q.e: Sleep loss produces hyperalgesia and reduces antinociceptive potency of morphine.

q.s: In the OPPERA cohort, adults with ≥2 OSA signs/symptoms had what increase in incidence of first-onset TMD?
q.e: ≥2 OSA signs/symptoms conferred a 73% greater incidence, independent of confounders, with OSA symptoms preceding TMD.

q.s: In the OPPERA case-control analysis, chronic TMD was how much more frequent in adults with a high versus low likelihood of OSA?
q.e: Chronic TMD was >3× more frequent in those with high likelihood of OSA.

q.s: Which is a proposed mechanism linking OSA with TMD?
o: Central sensitisation with impaired pain inhibition via reduced baroreflex sensitivity
q.e: Proposed mechanisms: central sensitisation (baroreflex), sympathetic activation and sleep bruxism.

q.s: The most appropriate way to describe the OSA–TMD relationship to a patient is:
o: A robust association with plausible mechanisms, not an established causal relationship
q.e: Association ≠ causation is one of the three exam-wide themes; overclaiming loses marks.

q.s: Heavy snoring is thought to have an independent adverse effect on which structure?
q.e: Vibration near the carotid bifurcation may cause endothelial injury and increased intima-media thickness.

q.s: Which metabolic consequence is linked with untreated OSA?
q.e: Intermittent hypoxia and fragmentation promote insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia and T2DM.

q.s: Which neurological outcome is associated with OSA?
q.e: OSA is linked to neurocognitive decline, dementia and stroke.

q.s: The impact of OSA on an individual’s quality of life includes:
o: Reduced quality of life, relationship difficulties from snoring and impaired alertness
q.e: Individual impacts span alertness, mood, relationships and quality of life.

q.s: Which pathophysiological process most directly links OSA to cardiovascular disease?
o: Repeated intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic activation
q.e: Intermittent hypoxia and recurrent sympathetic surges drive hypertension, arrhythmia and vascular injury.

q.s: Untreated severe OSA is associated with which mortality outcome?
q.e: Untreated OSA increases mortality and premature death.

q.s: Which pain-related effect of CPAP has been reported?
o: Decreased pain sensitivity and increased pain tolerance
Development of new TMD in most users
q.e: CPAP has been associated with reduced pain sensitivity and increased pain tolerance.

q.s: In the context of dental sleep medicine, the prevalence of TMD in OSA patients is reported as:
q.e: TMD in OSA is reported at 2–52%; OSA in TMD ~28%.

q.s: Which practical conclusion follows from the OSA–TMD evidence?
o: Screen for TMD before starting appliance therapy
Treat all TMD patients with CPAP
Never treat OSA patients with an appliance
q.e: The prevalence of TMD in OSA justifies baseline TMD screening before OAT.

q.s: Sleep bruxism is proposed as a mechanism linking OSA and TMD because:
o: It is more common in OSA and may contribute to masticatory muscle and joint overload
It is caused by mandibular advancement
It reduces the incidence of TMD
q.e: SB, commoner in OSA, is the third proposed mechanism for the OSA–TMD association.

q.s: Which societal consequence of OSA is of greatest public safety concern?
o: Increased risk of serious and fatal motor vehicle crashes
q.e: Impaired reflexes and judgement increase crash and workplace accident risk.

q.s: The economic impact of OSA includes:
o: Reduced productivity, lost work hours, more sick leave and greater healthcare use
q.e: OSA disproportionately affects the middle-aged workforce with lost productivity and greater health resource use.

q.s: Which population is disproportionately affected economically by OSA?
q.e: Economic burden falls disproportionately on middle-aged workers.

q.s: OSA is described as a public health issue because:
o: It affects society through safety, economic and healthcare burdens, not just the individual
q.e: Beyond the individual, OSA affects public safety, productivity and healthcare costs.

q.s: Which social consequence of untreated sleep disorders is described?
o: Social withdrawal and reduced desire for interaction, contributing to loneliness
q.e: Sleep disorders worsen depression and anxiety and contribute to withdrawal and loneliness.

q.s: A bus driver with suspected OSA reports falling asleep at traffic lights. The most appropriate dental response is:
o: Urgent referral to a physician with explicit advice about driving
Wait until the next routine recall
Fit an appliance immediately and advise he may continue driving
q.e: Sleepiness while driving in a commercial driver warrants urgent assessment and explicit driving advice.

q.s: Workplace safety concerns from OSA are greatest in:
o: Safety-critical occupations such as transport and heavy machinery operation
q.e: Sleepiness-related errors are most dangerous in safety-critical roles.

q.s: Which statement about OSA and healthcare costs is correct?
o: OSA has no effect on health spending
Untreated OSA increases healthcare resource use
q.e: Greater healthcare utilisation is a recognised societal burden.

q.s: Why is objective appliance compliance documentation particularly important for commercial transport workers?
o: It replaces the need for a diagnosis
It is only for insurance marketing
It may be required as legal proof of treatment for fitness-to-work purposes
q.e: Compliance data support legal and insurance documentation in safety-sensitive occupations.

q.s: Which is a societal consequence of insufficient sleep in adolescents?
o: Increased crash rate, particularly in young males
q.e: Adolescent sleep loss increases sleep-related crashes, especially in young males.

q.s: Snoring that disturbs the bed partner contributes to which societal or relational burden?
o: Bed-partner sleep deprivation, social disharmony and relationship difficulty
q.e: Snoring causes social disharmony and partner sleep deprivation, depression and fatigue.

q.s: Shift workers with untreated SDB are at particular risk of:
q.e: SDB compounds shift-work sleep disruption, increasing accident risk.

q.s: An employer asks whether OSA is relevant to occupational health. The best answer is:
o: Only if the employee snores at work
Yes — untreated OSA increases errors, accidents, absenteeism and work disability
q.e: OSA affects workplace safety, productivity and disability.

q.s: Which mental health effect of untreated sleep disorders has societal implications?
q.e: Sleep disorders worsen depression and anxiety, adding to societal burden.

q.s: Which feature distinguishes insomnia from short sleep duration?
o: Insomnia occurs only with inadequate opportunity for sleep
Short sleepers always have daytime impairment
Insomnia requires less than 5 hours of sleep
Insomnia requires daytime impairment despite adequate opportunity for sleep
q.e: A person who sleeps 5 hours and functions well is a short sleeper, not an insomniac.

q.s: ICSD-3/ICSD-3-TR criteria for chronic insomnia disorder require symptoms at least:
o: 3 nights per week for at least 3 months
q.e: ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months; the older “one month” criterion was ICSD-2/DSM-IV.

q.s: The “at least one month” duration criterion for chronic insomnia comes from:
q.e: Older material used one month; current criteria require three months.

q.s: Insomnia symptoms (without necessarily meeting disorder criteria) affect approximately:
Among patients with medical or psychiatric comorbidity, insomnia prevalence is approximately:
q.e: Insomnia is highly prevalent (50–75%) in comorbid populations.

q.s: The dominant pathophysiological model of chronic insomnia is:
o: Hyperarousal across both sleep and wake
q.e: Hyperarousal with heightened sympathetic and HPA-axis activity perpetuates insomnia.

q.s: Which finding is a recognised physiological correlate of insomnia?
o: Increased high-frequency (beta/gamma) EEG activity during NREM
q.e: Correlates include increased beta/gamma EEG, metabolic rate, cortisol/ACTH and body temperature.

q.s: First-line treatment for chronic insomnia disorder is:
q.e: CBT-I is first line, without tolerance or adverse drug effects.

q.s: Which CBT-I components have the strongest evidence?
q.e: Stimulus control and sleep restriction are the most evidence-supported of the five components.

q.s: Which CBT-I component is considered the weakest and insufficient as monotherapy?
q.e: Sleep hygiene alone is insufficient for chronic insomnia.

q.s: CBT-I typically produces marked improvements in all of the following EXCEPT:
o: A large immediate increase in total sleep time
q.e: TST improves only modestly initially, augmenting over time; SOL, WASO and SE improve markedly.

q.s: Which is a recognised risk factor for insomnia?
q.e: Risk factors include female sex, age, comorbidity, shift work, unemployment and low SES.

q.s: In children, insomnia (reported by caregivers) commonly presents as:
o: Bedtime resistance, frequent night awakenings and inability to sleep independently
q.e: Paediatric insomnia features bedtime resistance and difficulty sleeping independently.

q.s: Comorbid insomnia and sleep apnoea (COMISA) is best managed by:
o: Treating both conditions, e.g. CBT-I alongside OSA therapy
Treating the OSA only, as insomnia will resolve
q.e: Insomnia is a comorbid disorder warranting separate treatment; reducing AHI alone will not resolve the complaint.

q.s: Why are second-generation antipsychotics such as quetiapine increasingly used for insomnia?
o: Dissatisfaction with other options rather than evidence of superiority
They are first line in guidelines
q.e: Their increasing use reflects dissatisfaction, not evidence.

q.s: A characteristic PSG phenomenon in chronic insomnia is the “reverse first-night effect”, meaning:
o: REM appears only on the first night
Sleep is identical on both nights
Worse sleep on the first night than the second
Better sleep on the first laboratory night than the second
q.e: Insomniacs may sleep better in the novel lab environment on the first night.

q.s: PSG is NOT routinely indicated in chronic insomnia unless:
o: The patient has insomnia for more than 3 months
A breathing or movement disorder is suspected, diagnosis is uncertain or treatment has failed
q.e: PSG is reserved for suspected SDB/PLMD, diagnostic uncertainty, treatment failure or violent arousals.

q.s: Which is required for a diagnosis of insomnia?
o: At least one daytime impairment such as fatigue, mood disturbance or poor concentration
q.e: Both nocturnal symptoms and daytime dysfunction are required.

q.s: Short-term insomnia disorder refers to:
o: Clinically significant insomnia not meeting the frequency/duration criteria for chronic insomnia
q.e: Short-term insomnia disorder fails chronic frequency/duration thresholds but is clinically significant.

q.s: A central apnoea is defined by cessation of airflow for ≥10 s with:
q.e: The discriminator between central and obstructive apnoea is respiratory effort, detected by RIP belts.

q.s: Central sleep apnoea is considered the primary diagnosis when central apnoeas constitute at least:
q.e: CSA is primary when ≥50% of apnoeas are central.

q.s: A mixed apnoea is one that:
o: Begins as central and ends as obstructive
Begins as obstructive and ends as central
q.e: Mixed apnoeas start without effort and end with obstructed effort.

q.s: Cheyne–Stokes breathing is most commonly associated with:
q.e: Cheyne–Stokes respiration is a CSA pattern seen in heart failure and stroke.

q.s: Which drug class is a recognised cause of central sleep apnoea?
q.e: Opioids cause dose-dependent respiratory depression with central apnoeas and ataxic breathing.

q.s: Adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) is contraindicated in:
o: Symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
q.e: ASV is contraindicated in symptomatic HFrEF.

q.s: Non-hypercapnic central sleep apnoea is typically driven by:
q.e: Non-hypercapnic CSA reflects ventilatory instability (high loop gain).

q.s: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is defined by:
o: Obesity with normal awake CO2 and snoring
Obesity with awake hypercapnia not otherwise explained
q.e: OHS requires obesity with awake hypercapnia not attributable to another cause.

q.s: Catathrenia is best described as:
o: Slow, monotone, groaning expiratory vocalisation during sleep
q.e: Catathrenia is a benign expiratory groaning often mistaken for a parasomnia.

q.s: Upper airway resistance syndrome (UARS) typically presents in:
o: Young, non-obese women with fatigue and insomnia rather than sleepiness
Elderly obese men with severe hypoxaemia
q.e: UARS produces repetitive RERAs without qualifying events; ICSD-3 includes it within the OSA spectrum.

q.s: How does ICSD-3 classify UARS?
o: As part of the OSA spectrum captured by the RDI, not a separate entity
As a form of central apnoea
As a distinct disorder separate from OSA
q.e: ICSD-3 does not recognise UARS separately.

q.s: Primary snoring is defined as:
o: Snoring with excessive sleepiness and AHI >5
Habitual snoring without significant apnoea or oxygen desaturation
q.e: Primary snoring requires exclusion of OSA by a physician.

q.s: Which proportion of OSA patients do not snore?
q.e: ~⅓ of OSA patients don’t snore, and ~⅓ of snorers have no OSA.

q.s: Heavy snoring has been defined as snoring for more than what proportion of sleep time?
q.e: Heavy snoring (>50% of sleep time) may injure the carotid endothelium.

q.s: Which management of primary snoring was associated with an unacceptably high extrusion rate?
q.e: Palatal implants (three midline implants) had high extrusion, limited durability and potential to worsen OSA.

q.s: For primary snoring in a dentate patient, which treatment is described as first-line after assessment by both dentist and sleep physician?
q.e: MAD is first-line in dentate patients once OSA has been excluded.

q.s: CPAP pressures that typically abolish simple snoring are:
q.e: Low pressures of 4–6 cmH2O generally eliminate simple snoring.

q.s: A daily smartphone-based myofunctional regimen over 8 weeks reduced acoustically measured snoring rate by about:
q.e: The 15-min daily regimen reduced snoring rate by ~22% — low risk but significant commitment for modest gain.

q.s: In a sham-controlled study of snoring devices, a placebo (sham) device:
o: Was equivalent to a custom titratable MAD
q.e: A sham placebo exacerbated snoring, while custom titratable devices outperformed thermoplastic ones.

q.s: Positional therapy for snoring is effective in:
o: Most non-apnoeic supine-dominant snorers, but not those with OSA
Patients who snore in all positions
q.e: Positional devices reduce snoring in most non-apnoeic snorers (AHI <5) but not in OSA.

q.s: Which statement about benzodiazepines and snoring is correct?
o: They have no effect on the airway
They increase NREM snoring and upper airway resistance even in healthy people
They reduce snoring by deepening sleep
q.e: Benzodiazepine reduction is part of graded snoring management.

q.s: Nasal surgery as a primary anti-snoring procedure is:
o: Of uncertain and inconsistent benefit, but useful as a preliminary or adjunctive step
q.e: Septoplasty/turbinate reduction is indicated only with symptoms and objective obstruction, mostly as an adjunct.

q.s: Sleep-related hypoxaemia disorder is characterised by:
o: Sustained desaturation without a comparable rise in CO2
q.e: Distinguish from hypoventilation, where CO2 retention occurs.

q.s: The relationship between CSA and OSA is described as:
o: Bidirectional, with mixed pictures present in many sleep apnoea patients
q.e: Central events can provoke obstructive events in vulnerable anatomy and vice versa.

q.s: NREM parasomnias (disorders of arousal) typically arise from which stage?
q.e: Confusional arousals, sleepwalking and sleep terrors arise from N3 in the first third of the night.

q.s: Which feature is typical of NREM disorders of arousal?
o: Amnesia for the event, occurring in the first third of the night
Occurrence mainly in the last third of the night
q.e: Disorders of arousal are typically amnestic and early in the night; commoner in children.

q.s: REM sleep behaviour disorder is characterised by:
o: Loss of REM atonia with dream enactment
q.e: RBD involves loss of REM atonia and dream-enacting behaviour, typically in older men.

q.s: RBD is an important prodrome of which group of diseases?
o: Alpha-synucleinopathies (Parkinson’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, MSA)
Tauopathies such as Alzheimer’s disease only
q.e: RBD frequently precedes synucleinopathies; neurological evaluation is warranted.

q.s: Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder is most typical of:
q.e: Adolescents show a circadian phase delay; advanced phase is more typical of older adults.

q.s: Restless legs syndrome is characterised by:
o: An urge to move the legs, worse in the evening and at rest, relieved by movement
Leg jerks occurring only in REM sleep
q.e: RLS (Willis–Ekbom disease) is associated with iron deficiency and dopaminergic dysfunction.

q.s: RLS is associated with:
q.e: Iron deficiency and dopaminergic dysfunction underlie RLS.

q.s: An abnormal periodic limb movement index in adults is greater than:
q.e: PLMI >15/h in adults (>5/h in children); PLMD additionally requires associated sleep disturbance.

q.s: Narcolepsy type 1 is caused by:
o: Loss of hypocretin/orexin neurons, typically with cataplexy
q.e: NT1 = orexin deficiency with cataplexy; NT2 lacks cataplexy.

q.s: MSLT findings supporting narcolepsy are:
o: One SOREMP with latency of 20 min
Mean sleep latency ≥15 min with no SOREMPs
Mean sleep latency ≤8 min with ≥2 SOREMPs
q.e: MSL ≤8 min with ≥2 SOREMPs supports narcolepsy, though SOREMPs also occur in untreated OSA.

q.s: Which is classified as a central disorder of hypersomnolence?
q.e: Central hypersomnolence disorders include narcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnia, Kleine–Levin and insufficient sleep syndrome.

q.s: Sleep bruxism is grouped in the sleep disorder classification under:
q.e: Sleep bruxism and rhythmic movement disorder sit with RLS/PLMD as sleep-related movement disorders.

q.s: Recurrent isolated sleep paralysis and nightmare disorder are classified as:
q.e: Along with RBD, these are REM-related parasomnias.

q.s: Advanced sleep–wake phase disorder is most typical of:
q.e: Older adults tend toward early sleep and early waking.

q.s: A sleep study shows a patient entering sleep directly into REM. This most suggests:
q.e: Sleep-onset REM is a hallmark of narcolepsy (though can occur with sleep deprivation or OSA).

q.s: Which finding on PSG should prompt neurological referral rather than a change in appliance plan?
o: REM sleep without atonia consistent with RBD
q.e: RBD changes the referral pathway given its link with neurodegeneration.

q.s: Insufficient sleep syndrome should be considered when:
o: Sleepiness results from chronically curtailed time in bed
q.e: Insufficient sleep is a common cause of sleepiness and blunts perceived benefit of OSA treatment.

q.s: Shift work disorder and jet lag are classified as:
q.e: Both result from misalignment between the circadian clock and the required sleep schedule.

q.s: SSRIs and SNRIs characteristically:
o: Have no effect on sleep architecture
Suppress REM and prolong REM latency, and may induce RLS, bruxism and nightmares
q.e: Drug-induced sleep bruxism makes this class especially relevant to dentists.

q.s: Benzodiazepines alter sleep architecture by:
o: Increasing N2 and reducing REM and N3
q.e: Benzodiazepines improve sleep onset but increase N2 and reduce SWS and REM; dependence and cognitive effects are risks.

q.s: Alcohol before bed typically:
o: Increases REM in the first half
Shortens sleep latency, suppresses REM in the first half with rebound in the second, and worsens OSA
q.e: Alcohol fragments sleep and reduces dilator tone while blunting arousal.

q.s: Caffeine disrupts sleep primarily by:
q.e: Caffeine blocks adenosine (the mediator of sleep pressure); half-life ~5 h.

q.s: The approximate half-life of caffeine is:
q.e: With a ~5 h half-life, afternoon caffeine can still affect sleep.

q.s: Which effect of caffeine on sleep is dose-dependent?
q.e: Caffeine prolongs SOL, increases WASO and reduces SWS dose-dependently.

q.s: Suvorexant acts as:
q.e: Suvorexant blocks orexin signalling; ramelteon is a melatonin agonist.

q.s: Which agent is recommended AGAINST for treating chronic insomnia in AASM guidance?
q.e: OTC antihistamines, herbal/nutritional substances (melatonin, valerian, tryptophan) and barbiturates are recommended against.

q.s: Melatonin as a hypnotic for chronic insomnia is:
q.e: Melatonin as a hypnotic is among agents recommended against for chronic insomnia.

q.s: Why can a benzodiazepine be harmful in untreated OSA?
o: It reduces dilator tone and blunts arousal, causing longer and more frequent apnoeas
q.e: Sedatives raise the arousal threshold and relax the airway; the same mechanism is therapeutic only in the low-ArTH endotype with concurrent OSA treatment.

q.s: Opioid use in a patient with SDB results in a net:
o: Adverse effect, through respiratory depression and central apnoeas despite possible pain relief
q.e: Opioids impair architecture and respiratory control; the net effect in SDB is adverse.

q.s: Dexmedetomidine is noted for which sleep effect?
o: Improved sleep quality in ICU settings, with bradycardia and hypotension as adverse effects
q.e: It improves ICU sleep quality but can cause bradycardia and hypotension.

q.s: Sedating antidepressants such as low-dose doxepin and trazodone typically:
o: Reduce sleep latency and increase slow-wave sleep, with risk of long-term oversedation
q.e: Sedating antidepressants shorten latency and increase SWS.

q.s: Nicotine affects sleep by:
o: Acting as a stimulant and causing nocturnal withdrawal arousals
q.e: Nicotine is stimulating and withdrawal causes arousals; smoking also inflames the upper airway.

q.s: Sleep hygiene includes which recommendation?
o: Avoid caffeine, tobacco and heavy meals near bedtime and keep a regular schedule
Use devices in bed to relax
q.e: Sleep hygiene covers stimulants, alcohol, exercise timing, naps, time in bed and environment.

q.s: A patient taking an SSRI presents with new tooth wear and jaw pain on waking. The most relevant consideration is:
q.e: SSRIs/SNRIs can induce bruxism — a key pharmacological link for dentists.

q.s: Which medication class has been suggested (with an appropriate indication) for treatment of chronic insomnia?
o: Short/intermediate-acting benzodiazepine receptor agonists such as zolpidem or eszopiclone
q.e: Z-drugs, temazepam, ramelteon, suvorexant and sedating antidepressants are among suggested agents.

q.s: Eszopiclone (~3 mg) is being investigated in OSA to:
o: Raise the arousal threshold in the low-arousal-threshold endotype
q.e: Raising arousal threshold targets the “A” in PALM.

q.s: Polysomnography is best defined as:
o: A daytime nap test of sleep latency
A multi-parametric comprehensive recording of the biophysiological changes that occur during sleep
q.e: PSG records multiple physiological signals during sleep for research and diagnosis.

q.s: Which three channels together are required for sleep staging?
q.e: Without EEG, EOG and EMG no staging is possible — the fundamental limitation of level 3 and 4 studies.

q.s: The EOG channel in PSG is used mainly to:
o: Identify eye movements, REM sleep and sleep onset
q.e: Periorbital EOG electrodes record eye movements.

q.s: Which airflow sensor is used primarily to detect apnoeas?
q.e: The thermal sensor detects apnoea; the nasal pressure transducer is more sensitive for hypopnoea — ideally both are used.

q.s: Which airflow sensor is preferred for detecting hypopnoeas?
q.e: Nasal pressure is more sensitive to flow limitation but misses oral flow in mouth breathers.

q.s: Respiratory inductance plethysmography (RIP) belts are used to:
o: Measure thoracoabdominal respiratory effort and distinguish obstructive from central events
q.e: RIP is the recommended effort sensor for both laboratory and portable studies.

q.s: RIP measures respiration because breathing changes the circumference of the bands, which alters their:
q.e: Changes in cross-sectional area alter inductance, converted to a voltage proportional to thoracoabdominal volume.

q.s: Paradoxical thoracoabdominal movement on effort belts indicates:
q.e: Out-of-phase chest and abdominal movement occurs when the patient breathes against a closed airway.

q.s: Masseter EMG may be added to a PSG montage to assess:
q.e: Masseter EMG detects rhythmic masticatory muscle activity.

q.s: Tibial (anterior tibialis) EMG is recorded to detect:
Body position recording during PSG is particularly relevant to dental sleep medicine because:
o: Positional dependence influences appliance and positional therapy decisions
q.e: Supine vs non-supine AHI and % TST supine are directly actionable.

q.s: The snoring microphone in PSG is typically positioned:
o: At the foot of the bed
About 1 m above the head, recording frequency per hour and intensity in dB
q.e: Snoring is reported as frequency/hour and mean/maximum intensity in dB.

q.s: End-tidal or transcutaneous CO2 monitoring is a standard measurement in:
q.e: CO2 monitoring detects hypoventilation and is standard in children.

q.s: Normal sleep onset latency in adults is:
q.e: SOL and WASO are both normally <30 min.

q.s: Normal adult sleep efficiency is at least:
q.e: ≥85% normal (often >90% in young adults); 75–84% suboptimal; <75% suggests insomnia.

q.s: A sleep efficiency of 72% would most suggest:
Arousals on PSG are scored according to the ASDA rule of an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting at least:
q.e: The ASDA 3-second rule defines EEG arousals.

q.s: Normal oxygen saturation during sleep is:
q.e: Minimum SaO2 is an independent marker of severity.

q.s: Which parameter is reported as a percentage of total sleep time to judge positional dependence?
q.e: % TST supine is needed to judge positional dependence and sampling adequacy.

q.s: The oxygen desaturation index (ODI) counts:
o: Desaturations of ≥3% or ≥4% per hour of sleep
q.e: ODI quantifies desaturation events per hour.

q.s: Which statement about pulse oximetry in PSG is correct?
o: It uses a finger probe with high sampling rate and short signal averaging
q.e: Fast averaging is required to capture brief desaturations accurately.

q.s: In a normal PSG, NREM sleep dominates:
o: The first half of the night, with REM dominating the second half
The second half of the night
q.e: SWS concentrates early; REM lengthens later.

q.s: ECG in PSG is used to:
o: Monitor heart rate, rhythm and arrhythmias during respiratory events

q.s: Video and audio recording during PSG help to identify:
q.e: Video aids diagnosis of abnormal behaviours.

q.s: The normal adult apnoea–hypopnoea index is:
An apnoea is scored when airflow falls by at least:
The AASM recommended adult hypopnoea rule requires a ≥30% airflow reduction for ≥10 s with:
q.e: The ≥4% desaturation alternative became optional in Scoring Manual v3 (2023), though some payers still require it.

q.s: Which scoring rule became optional in AASM Scoring Manual version 3 (2023)?
q.e: Some payers still require the 4% rule; definitions affect AHI and prevalence comparisons.

q.s: A RERA is:
o: A desaturation of ≥4% without airflow change
Increasing respiratory effort or nasal pressure flattening leading to an arousal, not meeting apnoea/hypopnoea criteria
q.e: RERAs are counted in the RDI but not the AHI.

q.s: The respiratory disturbance index (RDI) is:
o: Apnoeas + hypopnoeas + RERAs per hour of sleep
q.e: RDI includes RERAs, so it is always ≥ AHI.

q.s: Which statement comparing AHI and RDI is always true?
o: AHI is always greater than RDI
RDI is greater than or equal to AHI
q.e: RERAs by definition do not meet apnoea/hypopnoea criteria, so adding them can only increase the index.

q.s: Moderate adult OSA corresponds to an AHI of:
A 50-year-old with an AHI of 32/h has:
Under ICSD-3-TR, OSA can be diagnosed in an asymptomatic adult when the AHI (or RDI) is at least:
A patient with AHI 8/h and unrefreshing sleep:
o: Does not meet criteria because AHI <15
Meets OSA criteria because AHI ≥5 is accompanied by symptoms
q.e: AHI ≥5 with symptoms (sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, insomnia, witnessed events) satisfies diagnosis.

q.s: Which is NOT a qualifying symptom for diagnosing OSA at an AHI between 5 and 15?
q.e: Qualifying features include sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, insomnia, gasping/choking and partner-reported apnoeas.

q.s: The PSG signature of sleep fragmentation in untreated OSA includes:
o: Increased arousal index and N1, with reduced slow-wave and REM sleep
q.e: Fragmentation shifts architecture toward light sleep.

q.s: An obstructive apnoea is distinguished from a central apnoea by:
o: Persistence of respiratory effort during the event
q.e: Effort continues in obstructive apnoea and is absent in central apnoea.

q.s: Which oxygen measure is considered an independent marker of OSA severity?
q.e: Desaturation is an independent severity measure, though gradation is not universally agreed.

q.s: In chronic insomnia, PSG may show:
o: Shortened sleep latency and increased N3
Prolonged sleep latency and/or WASO with reduced sleep efficiency
q.e: Increased SOL/WASO, increased N1, reduced SWS and increased beta/gamma power are typical.

q.s: Which variable is NOT part of the standard respiratory section of a PSG report?
q.e: Mallampati is a clinical examination finding, not a PSG variable.

q.s: The arousal index is defined as:
o: The number of arousals per hour of sleep
The percentage of sleep spent awake
The number of awakenings per night
q.e: Arousal index = arousals per hour of sleep.

q.s: A child aged 8 with an AHI of 6/h has:
q.e: Paediatric thresholds: <1 normal, 1–<5 mild, 5–<10 moderate, ≥10 severe.

q.s: A child with an obstructive AHI of 2/h has:
Above what age are adult scoring criteria generally applied?
q.e: 12 years is the commonly used cut-off for childhood SDB criteria.

q.s: In an older-literature definition, a hypopnoea was expressed as a reduction in airflow of:
q.e: Historically >50% reduction; current AASM criteria use ≥30% plus desaturation/arousal.

q.s: An event with a 95% airflow reduction for 15 s while thoracic and abdominal belts show continued, paradoxical movement is scored as:
q.e: ≥90% reduction ≥10 s with persistent effort is obstructive.

q.s: An event with complete absence of airflow for 12 s and flat effort belts, followed by resumption of breathing, is:
An event with a 40% airflow reduction for 14 s, accompanied by a 3% desaturation, is scored (AASM recommended rule) as:
q.e: ≥30% reduction ≥10 s with ≥3% desaturation meets the recommended hypopnoea rule.

q.s: An event with flattening of nasal pressure and increasing effort over 20 s, terminating in an arousal, without desaturation and with <30% flow reduction, is:
q.e: Effort-related arousal not meeting apnoea/hypopnoea criteria.

q.s: Why is the choice of hypopnoea definition (3% vs 4%) clinically important?
o: It has no effect on AHI
It changes only the arousal index
It changes the AHI, the severity category and reported prevalence
q.e: The 4% rule produces lower AHI values than the 3%/arousal rule.

q.s: Irregular or absent sleep stages on PSG may point to:
q.e: Narcolepsy patients may enter sleep directly into REM.

q.s: Which of the following is NOT a feature of fragmented sleep on PSG?
When reporting an AHI, which time is used as the denominator in an attended PSG?
q.e: AHI is per hour of sleep; home studies often use recording time, underestimating AHI.

q.s: When reading a sleep study, the single most actionable item for a dentist planning appliance therapy is often:
q.e: Supine dependence favours positional therapy and increases appliance success.

q.s: REM-predominant OSA responds relatively poorly to mandibular advancement because:
o: REM atonia defeats the mechanical advantage of the appliance
q.e: Warn patients and plan objective verification.

q.s: A patient’s PSG shows severe OSA with marked desaturation (nadir 74%) and coronary artery disease. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: CPAP first or combination therapy, with a low threshold for objective follow-up
q.e: Significant desaturation with CVD argues for CPAP first or combination therapy.

q.s: Oral appliance therapy is generally indicated for:
o: Severe OSA as first line in all patients
Mild–moderate OSA, or severe OSA where CPAP is refused, not tolerated or ineffective

q.s: Pharmacotherapy derived from PSG findings is appropriate mainly for:
o: Other disorders diagnosed on the study (e.g. RBD) or residual sleepiness
q.e: Drugs are not a primary OSA treatment.

q.s: A patient with a supine AHI of 28 and non-supine AHI of 3 is:
o: A candidate for positional therapy and a favourable appliance responder
q.e: Positional OSA (non-supine AHI <5) favours positional therapy and OAT.

q.s: A PSG shows the patient was supine for only 20% of the night with a low overall AHI. What is the main concern?
o: Supine sleep may have been under-sampled, underestimating usual AHI
q.e: Low supine time can under-sample positional disease.

q.s: Surgery is generally reserved for:
o: Severe disease intolerant of CPAP and appliances, particularly with correctable anatomical obstruction
q.e: Surgical options follow failure of conservative treatments.

q.s: Which PSG finding changes the referral pathway rather than the appliance design?
o: Central events, periodic limb movements or RBD

q.s: Why does severity on PSG matter to the dentist?
o: It sets the efficacy baseline and predicts appliance response
It replaces the need for physician referral
It is unrelated to appliance therapy
q.e: Higher AHI predicts lower likelihood of complete response with an appliance.

q.s: Weight loss as a behavioural recommendation is most strongly indicated from a PSG when:
o: The patient is supine-dependent but lean
q.e: Weight loss is appropriate where obesity contributes.

q.s: Compared with an oral appliance, CPAP has been shown in some studies to have a greater effect on:
q.e: CPAP is more efficacious for AHI, arousals and desaturation.

q.s: A dentist reviewing a PSG report should:
o: Make the OSA diagnosis from the report
Extract information relevant to the dental plan while leaving diagnosis to the physician
q.e: Read competently, extract what changes the plan, stop short of diagnosis.

q.s: High AHI (≥30) generally implies:
o: More aggressive treatment may be needed, with CPAP more often achieving AHI <5
q.e: Both treatments reduce AHI but complete response is more frequent with CPAP.

q.s: Which PSG pattern predicts a better response to mandibular advancement?
o: Severe hypoxaemia with high CPAP pressure
q.e: Positional and non-REM-dependent OSA respond better.

q.s: A high therapeutic CPAP pressure on titration implies:
o: A more collapsible airway and poorer appliance response
q.e: Lower required CPAP pressure predicts better appliance response.

q.s: A PSG reports AHI 12/h, minimum SaO2 91%, supine-predominant events and NREM-predominant pattern in a lean 40-year-old woman. Which statement is most accurate?
o: She has favourable predictors for oral appliance therapy
q.e: Mild OSA, lean, female, positional and NREM-predominant are all favourable predictors.

q.s: Behavioural therapies suggested by PSG findings include:
o: Positional therapy where supine-dependent and weight loss where obese

q.s: A PSG shows AHI 22/h with 60% central apnoeas. What is the appropriate dental response?
o: Fit a MAD at maximum protrusion
Refer back to the physician; this is primarily CSA, which an appliance does not treat
Proceed with appliance therapy as for OSA
q.e: Central events change the referral pathway, not the appliance.

q.s: When the PSG demonstrates periodic limb movements with arousals, the dentist should:
o: Inform the physician, as PLMs may contribute to symptoms independently of OSA treatment

q.s: A complete response to oral appliance therapy is defined as:
o: Resolution of OSA symptoms and treatment AHI <5/h
q.e: Complete response requires both symptom resolution and AHI <5.

q.s: A partial response is defined as:
o: Improved symptoms and ≥50% AHI reduction, but AHI remains ≥5/h
q.e: Partial response — improvement but residual disease.

q.s: Treatment failure is defined as:
o: Ongoing clinical symptoms, with or without <50% AHI reduction
q.e: Failure is defined by persistent symptoms.

q.s: A patient’s AHI falls from 30 to 12 with improved symptoms. This is:
q.e: 60% reduction with residual AHI ≥5 and improved symptoms.

q.s: A patient’s AHI falls from 25 to 18 and he remains sleepy. This is:
With successful OSA treatment, total sleep time on PSG typically:
o: Is unchanged, with redistribution toward more REM
q.e: Successful treatment redistributes sleep (REM rebound) rather than increasing it.

q.s: REM rebound after effective OSA treatment refers to:
o: An increase in REM sleep proportion after treatment
q.e: REM rises and NREM falls with treatment.

q.s: In a published PSG comparison of a mandibular advancement splint versus control, AHI changed from approximately:
q.e: Classic MAS results: AHI 30→14, min SaO2 87→91%, arousal index 41→27.

q.s: In that same comparison, which snoring variable was unchanged by the splint?
q.e: Frequency (402→242/h) and mean intensity fell; maximum intensity did not change.

q.s: In the MAS comparison, the arousal index changed from approximately:
q.e: Arousal index fell with the splint.

q.s: In the MAS comparison, REM as a percentage of total sleep time changed from approximately:
Which pattern indicates a good treatment outcome on PSG?
o: AHI reduced, minimum SaO2 increased, arousal index reduced

q.s: Why do published oral appliance efficacy figures vary widely (e.g. 37–95%)?
o: Different definitions of success are used
q.e: Cure (AHI <5), ≥50% reduction, AHI <10, or symptom improvement give very different numbers.

q.s: “Near-complete response” in some literature refers to:
q.e: Some papers use a looser AHI <10 threshold.

q.s: On a treatment PSG, minimum SaO2 in the MAS comparison improved from approximately:
A patient on an appliance reports feeling much better and snoring has stopped. Treatment PSG shows AHI 4/h. This represents:
q.e: Symptom resolution plus AHI <5 is complete response.

q.s: Which outcome measure is most suitable for confirming efficacy of an oral appliance in moderate OSA?
o: Dentist-performed oximetry interpreted by the dentist as final verification
Follow-up sleep study with the appliance in place at the final setting
q.e: Objective verification by the physician is required.

q.s: Effective treatment with an oral appliance typically produces which change in NREM sleep percentage?
A treatment PSG shows AHI 9/h, down from 40, with resolution of sleepiness. Using the three-category scheme this is:
q.e: AHI remains ≥5 despite >50% reduction and improved symptoms.

q.s: Total sleep time in the published MAS comparison was:
q.e: TST does not change significantly with effective treatment.

q.s: A Type 1 sleep study is:
o: A home study with 4–7 sensors without sleep staging
q.e: Type 1 is attended in-laboratory PSG with 15–20 sensors and ≥7 channels.

q.s: A Type 2 sleep study is:
o: An unattended full-montage PSG, usually at home
q.e: Type 2 has the full montage (10–15 sensors) without a technician.

q.s: A Type 3 study typically:
o: Monitors breathing parameters with 4–7 sensors but without sleep staging
q.e: Type 3 records airflow, effort, oximetry and heart rate without EEG.

q.s: A Type 4 study records:
o: 1–2 bioparameters, typically oximetry ± airflow or heart rate

q.s: The approximate number of sensors used in a Type 1 study is:
A home Type 2 study tends to:
o: Be identical to a Type 1 study in all cases
q.e: Loss of effort signals and use of recording time as denominator cause underestimation.

q.s: The approximate failure rate of Type 2 home studies is:
q.e: Failure is more likely when wired unsupervised.

q.s: A symptomatic patient with loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and ESS 15 has a home study showing AHI 4/h. The correct next step is:
o: Repeat a Type 4 oximetry study at home
Refer back to the physician for in-laboratory PSG; do not accept the negative result
q.e: A negative home study in a symptomatic patient cannot exclude OSA.

q.s: Which statement about the direction of home study error is correct?
o: A positive home study can generally be believed; a negative one in a symptomatic patient cannot
A negative home study rules out OSA
A positive home study must always be repeated in the lab

q.s: Type 1 PSG is indicated rather than Type 2 when:
o: Central sleep apnoea, hypoventilation, parasomnia or a movement disorder is suspected
The patient has high pre-test probability of uncomplicated moderate–severe OSA
q.e: Complex or non-OSA disorders need attended PSG.

q.s: Type 2 home studies are best suited to patients with:
o: High probability of moderate–severe OSA without significant comorbidity or other suspected sleep disorder
q.e: Uncomplicated high-probability OSA suits home testing.

q.s: Which patient factor mandates Type 1 rather than Type 2 testing?
o: Severe intellectual disability or major communication difficulty
q.e: Patient factors include disability, neuromuscular disease, unsuitable home environment and medicolegal implications.

q.s: An advantage of attended Type 1 PSG is:
o: Real-time sensor troubleshooting and accurate staging
q.e: Supervision allows correction of sensor problems and comfort interventions.

q.s: A disadvantage of attended Type 1 PSG is:
o: Expense, labour intensity and the unfamiliar environment affecting sleep
q.e: Laboratory testing is costly and may disturb sleep, especially in children.

q.s: An advantage of home Type 2 studies is:
o: More representative sleep in a familiar environment and improved access
q.e: Home testing is cost-effective and accessible.

q.s: In Australia, which statement about Type 3 and 4 studies is noted in the revision material?
o: MBS reimbursement is not available for them, so use has been limited
They are the only reimbursed tests
They are used for paediatric diagnosis
They are required before all PSG
q.e: A jurisdiction-specific point; state the principle first and the local rule second.

q.s: Types 3 and 4 studies can confirm OSA only in:
o: Highly selected patients with high pre-test probability of moderate–severe disease without significant comorbidity
q.e: Limited-channel tests are for selected patients.

q.s: Which is a limitation of Type 3 studies compared with Type 1?
o: No sleep staging, so the denominator is recording time and arousal-based hypopnoeas are missed
q.e: Without EEG, arousals and sleep time cannot be scored.

q.s: Which home testing setting has the highest failure rate?
o: Wired in the laboratory then sent home, or self-applied unsupervised
q.e: Unsupervised setups are more prone to signal loss.

q.s: Type 1 PSG is the standard investigation for:
o: Routine appliance titration by the dentist
Narcolepsy, central sleep apnoea, parasomnias and movement disorders
q.e: Attended PSG is required for these disorders.

q.s: Why might a laboratory PSG be particularly difficult for children?
o: Paediatric AHI cannot be scored in a laboratory
Children cannot be wired for EEG
The unfamiliar environment and strange technician are stressful, affecting sleep and cooperation
q.e: Despite this, attended PSG remains the paediatric gold standard.

q.s: A home Type 2 study is valid for diagnosing OSA only when:
o: Ordered by any clinician without evaluation
Used for screening the general population
Used in conjunction with a comprehensive sleep evaluation and well-defined symptoms

q.s: Which is a Type 1 indication relating to prior testing?
o: A failed or inconclusive Type 2 study
q.e: Failed home studies should proceed to attended PSG.

q.s: Serious medicolegal consequences of a diagnosis (e.g. a commercial pilot) favour:
q.e: Medicolegal implications mandate the most reliable test.

q.s: Which home study feature contributes to AHI underestimation?
o: Using sleep time as the denominator
Using recording time rather than sleep time as the denominator
q.e: Recording time includes wake, diluting the index.

q.s: The Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) measures:
o: The tendency to fall asleep when given the opportunity
q.e: MSLT asks the patient to try to sleep; MWT asks them to stay awake.

q.s: The Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT) is mainly used to:
q.e: MWT assesses the ability to maintain wakefulness.

q.s: The MSLT should be preceded by:
o: An overnight PSG to confirm adequate prior sleep
A day of total sleep deprivation
q.e: Prior night PSG ensures results are interpretable.

q.s: How many nap opportunities are given in a standard MSLT?
o: Four to five at about 2-hour intervals

q.s: In an MSLT, each nap trial is terminated after how long if no sleep occurs?
q.e: Trials end at 20 min without sleep; the clinical version continues 15 min after sleep onset to allow REM.

q.s: In the clinical MSLT, after sleep onset the nap is continued for:
o: 15 minutes to allow REM to emerge

q.s: In the MWT the patient is instructed to:
o: Lie in the dark and try to fall asleep
Sit in a dimly lit room and try to stay awake
q.e: MWT measures ability to resist sleep.

q.s: Modern MWT protocols commonly terminate each trial after:
q.e: Older protocols used 20 min; modern ones 40 min.

q.s: A longer mean sleep latency on the MWT indicates:
Which statement about SOREMPs is correct?
o: They support narcolepsy but are also frequent in untreated OSA
q.e: SOREMPs lack specificity in untreated OSA.

q.s: Which factor shortens mean sleep latency on the MSLT?
q.e: Sleep loss shortens latency; stimulants, anxiety and anticipation lengthen it.

q.s: Which factor lengthens mean sleep latency on the MSLT?
q.e: CNS arousal and stimulants prolong latency.

q.s: The “last-nap effect” refers to:
o: REM appearing only in the first nap
Longer latency on the fifth nap, increasing mean latency in five-nap protocols
Shorter latency on the first nap
Failure to sleep in any nap
q.e: Anticipation of leaving lengthens the final nap latency.

q.s: A floor effect is a limitation of which test?
q.e: MSLT has a floor effect; MWT a ceiling effect.

q.s: An indication for the MSLT is:
o: Evaluating persistent sleepiness after OSA treatment
q.e: MSLT quantifies physiological sleepiness in narcolepsy, IH and residual sleepiness.

q.s: Which statement about MSLT/MWT limitations is correct?
o: Neither perfectly predicts real-world alertness or driving performance
Normative data are abundant in children
The MSLT alone certifies treatment response

q.s: A high “sleepability” individual may show which MSLT result even after two weeks of 10 h time in bed?
How does age affect MSLT latencies?
o: Longest in prepubescent children, shorter in young adults, longer again in older age

q.s: What is the relationship between prior-night total sleep time and next-day MSL?
o: Negative correlation in the sense that less prior sleep produces shorter latency
More prior sleep produces shorter latency

q.s: Between MWT trials patients should:
o: Remain in bed in the dark

q.s: Since 2017 the ADA policy on dentists and sleep-related breathing disorders states that:
o: All dentists should screen patients for SRBD
q.e: Screening is a core role for all dentists.

q.s: The dentist’s role in OSA is precisely to:
o: Order and interpret PSG for diagnosis
Screen for signs and symptoms and refer to a physician for diagnosis
q.e: Dentists are not authorised to diagnose SRBD.

q.s: Sensitivity of a screening test is:
o: The proportion without disease who test negative
The probability that a positive result is true
The proportion of people with the disease who test positive
q.e: A highly sensitive test, when negative, helps rule out disease.

q.s: Specificity of a screening test is:
o: The proportion of people without the disease who test negative
The proportion with disease who test positive
q.e: A highly specific test, when positive, helps rule in disease.

q.s: OSA screening questionnaires generally have:
o: Good but not optimal sensitivity and poor specificity, producing many false positives
q.e: They trigger referral but cannot diagnose.

q.s: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale consists of:
An ESS score indicating excessive daytime sleepiness is:
Why should the ESS never be used alone to screen for OSA?
o: It correlates poorly with AHI and sleepiness has many causes
It is only validated in children
q.e: It measures sleep propensity, not disease severity.

q.s: In STOP-BANG, “P” stands for:
q.e: Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnoea, Pressure, BMI, Age, Neck, Gender.

q.s: The BMI threshold used in STOP-BANG is:
q.e: BMI >35, age >50, neck >40 cm, male gender.

q.s: The STOP-BANG score indicating increased OSA risk is:
q.e: Higher cut-offs increase specificity at the cost of sensitivity.

q.s: Raising the STOP-BANG cut-off from 3 to 5 would:
OSA50 awards 3 points for waist circumference above:
o: 80 cm in men or 70 cm in women
94 cm in men or 80 cm in women
102 cm in men or 88 cm in women
110 cm in men or 100 cm in women
q.e: OSA50: waist 3, snoring 3, witnessed apnoeas 2, age ≥50 years 2; positive ≥5/10.

q.s: The OSA50 positive threshold is:
OSA50 performance for moderate–severe OSA is reported as:
q.e: The classic “sensitive but not specific” illustration.

q.s: The Berlin questionnaire classifies a patient as high risk when positive in:
q.e: Categories: snoring severity, daytime sleepiness, hypertension/obesity.

q.s: The NoSAS score suggests high probability of OSA at:
q.e: Neck >40 cm 4, BMI ≥30 5, snoring 2, age >55 4, male 2.

q.s: In the NoSAS score, the item carrying the most points (5) is:
q.e: BMI ≥30 scores 5; neck and age 4 each; snoring and male 2 each.

q.s: In the Australian Medicare direct-referral pathway, a GP may order a sleep study if the patient has a positive questionnaire plus an ESS of at least:
q.e: Positive Berlin, OSA50 ≥5 or STOP-BANG ≥4, plus ESS ≥8 — a jurisdiction-specific rule.

q.s: A significant caveat of the Australian direct-referral criteria is that:
o: Many patients with significant OSA will not meet the combination
q.e: Non-sleepy OSA patients may not qualify.

q.s: The modified Mallampati is performed with the patient:
o: Seated upright, mouth wide open, tongue protruded maximally without phonation
q.e: “Without phonation” distinguishes it from the original anaesthetic technique.

q.s: Modified Mallampati class III shows:
o: Soft palate, uvula, fauces and pillars
Soft palate and majority of uvula
Soft palate and base of the uvula only

q.s: Modified Mallampati class IV shows:
o: Soft palate and base of uvula
q.e: Class IV: only the hard palate is visible.

q.s: Scalloping (crenation) of the lateral tongue borders suggests:
o: A tongue too large for the arch (macroglossia), causing oropharyngeal crowding
q.e: Scalloping is the practical clinical sign of relative macroglossia.

q.s: Which uvula dimensions have been linked directly to SDB?
o: Longer than 15 mm and wider than 10 mm
q.e: An enlarged uvula >15 mm long and >10 mm wide is associated with SDB.

q.s: Dental erosion noted at a screening visit may indicate:
o: GORD, which frequently coexists with OSA
q.e: Erosion may signal reflux, a common OSA comorbidity.

q.s: A negative screening questionnaire in a patient with witnessed apnoeas and resistant hypertension should lead to:
o: Referral anyway, because a negative screen does not exclude OSA
q.e: Clinical suspicion overrides a negative screen.

q.s: The Paediatric Sleep Questionnaire is positive when the score exceeds:
q.e: PSQ >0.33 suggests high likelihood of SDB.

q.s: Large mandibular tori are relevant to OSA screening because they:
o: Reduce oral volume and displace the tongue posteriorly
q.e: Tori reduce oral volume, crowding the tongue.

q.s: Which radiographic/cephalometric finding is associated with increased OSA risk?
o: Inferiorly positioned hyoid and narrowed posterior airway space
q.e: Low hyoid and narrow PAS are risk markers.

q.s: Who first described the “monobloc” appliance, and in what year?
q.e: Robin described the monobloc in 1903 to treat glossoptosis.

q.s: Pierre Robin’s monobloc was originally designed to treat:
q.e: Glossoptosis — a posteriorly displaced tongue obstructing the airway.

q.s: The tongue retaining device was described by:
q.e: The TRD holds the tongue forward by suction.

q.s: Meier-Ewert and colleagues (1985) described:
o: An intraoral protraction device for sleep apnoea
q.e: Their work was part of the 1980s catalyst for modern OAT.
