q.s: George Catlin (19th century) is credited with suggesting that:
o: Nasal rather than mouth breathing produces more restful sleep and better health
q.e: Catlin first linked breathing mode to sleep quality.

q.s: After Robin’s 1903 work, approximately how long was there little development in oral appliances?
q.e: Roughly half a century of little development followed.

q.s: Historically, the tongue retaining device has been described as:
o: The most common oral appliance today
The second most common type of oral appliance
q.e: MADs are most common; TRDs historically second, now used rarely.

q.s: Which type of oral appliance is described as obsolete today?
q.e: Soft palate lifters are no longer in use.

q.s: According to AADSM terminology, an oral appliance is:
o: A device intended to protrude and stabilise the mandible to maintain a patent airway during sleep
A device that increases vertical dimension only
q.e: AADSM definition of an oral appliance.

q.s: A custom oral appliance is defined as one that:
o: Is a boil-and-bite device moulded at home
Is fabricated from digital or physical impressions/models, not prefabricated, of biocompatible material and engaging both arches

q.s: A titratable oral appliance is one that:
o: Allows the amount of mandibular protrusion to be varied
Holds the mandible in one fixed position
q.e: Titration of protrusion is the analogue of CPAP pressure titration.

q.s: Under the AADSM (2019) definition, an effective oral appliance must allow advancement in increments of:
The AADSM effective appliance definition requires a protrusive adjustment range of at least:
q.e: ≥5 mm range, reversibility and a verifiable setting.

q.s: Which is NOT part of the AADSM (2019) definition of an effective oral appliance?
o: Reversal of advancement must be possible
It maintains a stable retentive relationship to teeth, implants or ridge
It must be made of nylon
q.e: Material is not specified; the criteria concern titration, range, reversibility, verifiability, retention and regulatory clearance.

q.s: The evidence base for oral appliances evolved from:
o: Case reports to randomised controlled trials confirming efficacy
q.e: RCTs confirmed efficacy in mild–moderate and later severe OSA.

q.s: The tongue retaining device works by:
o: Holding the tongue forward in a bulb by suction
q.e: The pliable bulb holds the protruded tongue by negative pressure.

q.s: When is a tongue retaining device indicated?
o: For patients with severe nasal obstruction
When dental factors preclude a mandibular advancement device
q.e: TRDs are used rarely, e.g. edentulous or inadequate dentition.

q.s: A mandibular advancement device improves a soft palate-level obstruction by:
o: Increasing palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus tension, drawing the soft palate anteriorly and inferiorly

q.s: The predominant structural airway change with mandibular advancement is enlargement:
o: In the lateral dimension at the velopharyngeal level
q.e: Traction via soft tissue connections between pharynx and ramus widens the velopharynx laterally.

q.s: Tongue base advancement with a MAD results from:
o: Increased tension in suprahyoid and genioglossus muscles and hyoid stabilisation
q.e: The tongue is held forward via muscular attachments.

q.s: Which statement about the effect of mandibular advancement on PALM traits is correct?
o: It reduces collapsibility without systematically changing loop gain or arousal threshold
q.e: Its effect is on passive anatomy.

q.s: Mandibular advancement enlarges which airway segment besides the velopharynx?
The effect of increasing mandibular protrusion on airway collapsibility is:
q.e: Greater advancement → greater reduction in collapsibility (to a point).

q.s: The commonest site of tongue collapse that a TRD aims to prevent is:
q.e: Forward tongue posture prevents collapse into the oropharynx.

q.s: Mandibular advancement devices may be designed as:
o: One-piece or dual-component with a coupling mechanism

q.s: The hyoid bone during mandibular advancement is:
o: Stabilised and drawn forward with the mandible
q.e: Forward mandibular movement stabilises the hyoid.

q.s: Which explains why mild OSA suits mandibular advancement better than severe OSA?
o: Less collapsible airways and greater pharyngeal enlargement along the whole length
Higher loop gain in mild OSA

q.s: Imaging studies of mandibular advancement show that velopharyngeal enlargement occurs principally through:
o: Traction on soft tissue connections between the pharynx and mandibular ramus
Direct compression of the soft palate
q.e: Lateral pharyngeal wall traction is key.

q.s: A mandibular advancement device is best described physiologically as:
o: An anatomical intervention improving passive pharyngeal anatomy
q.e: It acts on the “P” of PALM.

q.s: Which statement about MAD mechanism is incorrect?
o: The appliance works simply by pulling the tongue forward, with no effect on the palate
It advances the jaw and attached musculature
q.e: It remodels the whole velo-oropharyngeal segment.

q.s: The net effect of OAT on the airway is:
o: Improved passive pharyngeal anatomy and reduced collapsibility

q.s: In a patient with high loop gain and a very collapsible airway, further mandibular advancement is likely to:
o: Add side effects without fixing the ventilatory control problem
q.e: Non-anatomical traits need other or combined therapies.

q.s: Oral appliance therapy is indicated for primary snoring when:
o: OSA has been excluded by a physician
The patient requests it, without a sleep assessment
q.e: Snoring cannot be clinically distinguished from OSA; diagnosis must come first.

q.s: According to AADSM 2025 standards, oral appliances are indicated for:
q.e: AADSM 2025 states appliances are indicated across severities, with CPAP considered first in severe disease.

q.s: For severe OSA, oral appliance therapy is appropriate when:
o: CPAP is refused, not tolerated, ineffective or the patient is unsuitable for CPAP
q.e: An IPD meta-analysis supports comparable health outcomes in severe OSA.

q.s: Which is a contraindication to mandibular advancement therapy?
o: Maximum protrusive range less than 6 mm
q.e: Limited protrusion <6 mm is a contraindication.

q.s: Which statement about TMD and OAT is correct?
